summary: Requests allocation of the application/mbox media type and defines a default format for the mbox database that all conforming implementations must support. Mbox is a way of storing email messages together in a file. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine keeping many letters in one long scroll, one after another. This memo gives that scroll a name so programs know what it is and how to read it.

subtitle: The MIME type and standard format for mailbox files containing email messages.

tldr.problem: For decades, UNIX systems have stored email messages in mbox files (files with many messages concatenated sequentially), but there was no standard MIME media type for them and no authoritative format specification, leading to incompatibility.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the application/mbox media type with IANA and defines a default format for mbox files: a linear sequence of Internet messages (per RFC 2822), each preceded by a separator line and terminated by an empty line.
tldr.outcome: Mbox files can now be exchanged over the network and between programs with a clear, standardized format. Programs know to expect RFC 2822-compliant messages in UTF-8, with a defined separator format.

facts.label: Message standard
facts.value: RFC 2822 compliant messages, seven-bit with proper encoding for eight-bit data

today: RFC 4155 is an Internet Standard informational specification. The application/mbox media type is now registered with IANA, and the default format is widely recognized. However, legacy mbox files predating this RFC often deviate from the strict format, and modern email clients have largely moved to other storage formats like Maildir. The RFC remains useful for historical data exchange and archiving.

sections.title: Background and the mbox Problem
sections.content:
The mbox format has been used for decades on UNIX systems as a way to store a linear sequence of email messages in a single file. A folder of messages becomes one file with many messages concatenated together. Despite its widespread use across many platforms and tools, there was no authoritative specification and no MIME media type.

The lack of standardization meant incompatibility: different tools formatted the separator lines differently, used different timestamp formats, and handled special cases like lines starting with 'From' differently. Exchanging mbox files across systems or between programs was risky because the format was ambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: Many programs store email by stacking letters in a file, one after another. For a long time, nobody agreed on exactly how to stack them, so moving a file between programs could lose or corrupt messages.

sections.title: Mbox Format Variations and the Default Format
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs the variations found in the wild: separator lines can use different timestamp formats, email addresses can use non-standard syntax, and some systems escape lines beginning with 'From' to avoid confusion while others do not.

To establish a baseline, the RFC defines a strict 'default' format that all compliant implementations must support: each message must be RFC 2822-compliant, using only seven-bit characters with eight-bit data properly encoded. Messages must be separated by a line containing the exact text 'From', a space, the sender's email address, another space, and a timestamp in UNIX ctime format (UTC, no timezone). Each message is terminated by an empty line. This format is simple and unambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule: each letter must be properly written (RFC 2822 format), start with 'From sender@example.com timestamp', and end with a blank line. Simple and clear.

sections.title: MIME Type Registration and the Format Parameter
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type as application/mbox in the IANA registry. It defines an optional 'format' parameter to allow for variations: application/mbox;format=default uses the strict format defined in the RFC, while other format values can be registered in future RFCs.

Implementations MUST support the default format. If an mbox file lacks a format parameter, it is implicitly 'default'. If the format parameter has an unknown value, systems SHOULD treat it as opaque binary data (application/octet-stream), since the format is not understood.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name is application/mbox. You can add a tag like format=default to say what kind of mbox it is. If you don't know the kind, treat it as mystery data.

sections.title: Encoding and Interoperability Considerations
sections.content:
A key concern: when an mbox file is sent as an email attachment, the recipient might store it in their own mbox mailstore. If the attachment's separator lines are not properly encoded, they might be confused with real separators in the recipient's file, causing messages to become irreversibly intermingled.

The RFC therefore requires that mbox files transferred via email MUST use transparent encoding like BASE64 or Quoted-Printable to protect the separator lines. Other transfer methods are encouraged to do the same. The RFC also notes that multipart/digest (defined in RFC 2046) is a better choice when transferring multiple RFC 2822 messages because it uses neutral, strict rules and is far more portable than mbox.
sections.plainLanguage: If you mail an mbox file to someone, scramble it (BASE64 or Quoted-Printable) so the mailbox program does not get confused. Better yet, use multipart/digest instead.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The RFC identifies mbox files as passive data with no unique security threats beyond the general risk of sharing any data. However, unintended information (user addresses, message history, site-specific encoding or language settings) can leak when sharing mbox files.

The RFC also notes that detection of mbox files by 'magic number' (looking for lines beginning with 'From ') is unreliable because the format is not authoritative. Implementations must be prepared to receive non-compliant data tagged as application/mbox and should be defensive in parsing. The default format is strict to allow robust parsing; other formats can be more lenient if registered in future specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing someone's mail file could reveal private stuff. Don't trust the file extension or magic number to tell you what kind of mbox it is; always check the format parameter.
